idea: Halftone close-up of a compositor's hand holding a composing stick full of metal type, letters mirror-reversed, captioned 'Backwards, upside down, and correct.' Hand compositors really did read type that way, and the shirt is for anyone who knows that doing things right can look wrong from outside.

Archive photo of a Linotype operator at the keyboard, captioned 'ETAOIN SHRDLU'. Those are the first two columns of Linotype keys, laid out roughly by letter frequency, and the phrase sometimes ended up in newspapers when operators ran a finger down the keys to fill out a botched line. It's an inside joke for type nerds.

Straight-on photo of a printer's type cases on their rack, captions 'UPPER CASE' and 'lower case' pointing at the top and bottom drawers. Capitals really were kept in the upper case. It's a small origin story people love explaining to friends.

Halftone of rows of brass-handled Library of Congress card catalog drawers, captioned 'Search engine, 1901.' That was the year the Library began selling its printed catalog cards to other libraries, and the shirt is a dry tribute to metadata done by hand.

Macro photo of round glass-topped typewriter keys showing Q W E R T Y, captioned 'Arranged in the 1870s. Never rearranged.' The QWERTY layout dates to the Sholes and Glidden typewriter, so this is a quiet comment on how long a temporary fix can last.
Close-up of a bookbinder's hands sewing folded signatures on a sewing frame, captioned 'Held together by thread.' It's true of every sewn book and of most other things worth keeping.
Archive photo of a telegraph operator's hand on a Morse key, captioned 'Charged by the word.' Telegrams really were billed per word, which made people terse. It's for people who believe in editing.

Close-up of a stenographer's notebook covered in Gregg shorthand loops, uncaptioned except for a small line underneath: 'Faster than talking.' Trained shorthand writers could keep up with speech, and to everyone else the page looks like beautiful nonsense.

Raking-light halftone of a braille page with every dot casting a shadow, captioned 'Read with the hand.' Louis Braille first published his system in 1829, as a teenager. Printed in one ink, the shirt turns touch into something you look at.

Old public-domain photograph of the Rosetta Stone, captioned 'Same decree, three scripts.' The stone carries one Ptolemaic decree in hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek, which made it the key to reading hieroglyphs. It's a shirt about translation as a way to unlock things.

Halftone close-up of a clay cuneiform tablet covered in wedge marks, captioned 'The first writing was bookkeeping.' The earliest proto-cuneiform tablets from Uruk are overwhelmingly administrative records of grain, livestock and labor. The idea that literature came after the receipts is funny and humbling.
FSA-era photo of a sign painter hand-lettering a storefront window, captioned 'Kerning by eye.' It's for designers who know software never fully replaced a steady hand.

Photo of an oversized wooden-type ampersand from a printer's drawer, captioned 'Once recited at the end of the alphabet.' Schoolchildren really did finish the ABCs with '... X, Y, Z, and per se and', which became the word 'ampersand'.

The 19th-century photograph of James Murray in his Scriptorium, surrounded by pigeonholes of quotation slips, captioned 'Defined by volunteers.' The Oxford English Dictionary was built on slips mailed in by readers from the public, so this is crowdsourcing before it had a name.

Close-up halftone of a page from the Library of Congress's Gutenberg Bible, one of the three perfect copies on vellum, captioned 'Printed c. 1455. Still legible.' It's a quiet challenge to every file format.

Close-up of a proofreader's marked-up galley with one deletion crossed out and 'stet' in the margin, with only the word 'stet' below. It's Latin for 'let it stand', the editor's mark for undoing a change, and the shirt is for people who learned that the first version was right.

An extreme enlargement of a 19th-century newspaper photograph, blown up until it falls apart into halftone dots, captioned 'Every picture is just dots that agreed.' Newspapers began printing halftone photographs in the 1880s, and the shirt is itself printed in halftone, so it's a joke about itself.

Archive photograph of a page from the Voynich manuscript, with its unknown script and odd plants, captioned 'Still unread.' Its writing has never been convincingly deciphered. It's for people who like to be reminded that some problems are still open.

US Marine Corps public-domain photo of two Navajo code talkers at a field radio in the Pacific, captioned 'A language, not a cipher.' The Navajo code was built on a living language and was never broken during the war. The shirt honors the speakers and the point that a language is worth more than a trick.

Early-1900s photo of clerks sorting mountains of envelopes in the US Post Office's Dead Letter Office, captioned 'Dead Letter Office.' It was a real department for mail that couldn't be delivered, and the shirt is a melancholy, beautiful image about all the words that never arrived.
